items.body: Structura Parva — literally “small structure” — acts as both title and manifesto. Seven years after Forma, the Italian duo Filtro (Luca de Biasi and Angelo Bignamini) have moved away from long-form improvisations built from concrete sounds and electrical interference towards something more concentrated, deliberate, and architectural. Across six concise pieces, they construct miniature sonic ecosystems from the sparsest of materials, embracing self-imposed limitations as catalysts for invention. Working with only a handful of sounds per track, Filtro adopt an approach reminiscent of Oulipo’s creative constraints, treating composition as a process of exploring the possibilities contained within a tightly defined framework. Yet the result never feels academic. The sounds themselves remain stubbornly alive: intermittent clicks, fragile drones, processed acoustic fragments and high-frequency traces evolve, misbehave and interact in ways that resist predictable looping or repetition. Rather than expanding ideas through scale, Filtro trace how small gestures ripple through space, giving the EP a sense of depth and movement. What distinguishes Structura Parva is its refusal of sonic flattening. Every sound retains its material presence and tactile character, whether emerging from a sampler, field recordings or processed everyday objects. The duo’s attention to dynamics and spatial placement ensures that even the sparsest passages feel animated by hidden tensions. These are not static minimal compositions but living structures, constantly shifting beneath the surface. The EP’s subtitle of sorts — “sounds for night reflections and dark disquiets” — feels apt. There is a subdued melancholy running throughout the record, but also curiosity and attentiveness. By reducing their palette and abandoning improvisation in favour of meticulous composition, Filtro have created their most focused work to date: a quietly compelling study in how much emotional weight can be carried by the smallest of structures. In the following interview Angelo Bignami and Luca de Biasi explain their working process. Structura Parva feels like a significant shift from the long-form improvisation for concrete sounds and electrical interferences of Forma towards much shorter and more concentrated pieces. What led you to embrace these “small structures”? Was this reduction a deliberate aesthetic decision or the natural outcome of your evolving practice? Luca de Biasi: After Forma, we took a long break to dedicate ourselves to our solo work, which also gave us the opportunity to reflect on what we wanted Filtro to become. The idea was to work meticulously on individual sounds, processing them and finding affinities with other sounds to shape the pieces. We set a strict limit: just two sounds each and nothing else. The biggest change for me was using a sampler, which allowed me to process sound differently than in the past and focus on individual sounds before looking at the whole picture. We also worked extensively on dynamics and the movement of sound in space. In some tracks, this remained direct, while in others we added the natural echoes of the different environments where we re-recorded the pieces. Angelo Bignamini: It was a bit of both. It represents an evolution of our sound, moving away from what were initially uncontrolled, improvisation-based impulses toward actual composition focused on a few core elements. I believe this shift was influenced by our shared listening habits at the time, as well as a mutual desire to produce something more focused and structured. The EP is described as reflecting a new approach to “minimal structures and small electronics.” What does “small electronics” mean for Filtro in practical and conceptual terms? Are you interested in intimacy, scale, fragility, or perhaps a different relationship between sound and space? L: The new approach was all about working on individual sounds before the whole composition. In practice, I used a modular synthesizer consisting simply of an oscillator, a complex envelope, and a filter, constantly tweaking the sound until I achieved a satisfactory result. I did the same using very simple field recordings. As I mentioned, the choice of individual sounds, their interaction, and their interconnectivity were the core ideas behind the project. A: It is called “small electronics” simply because the entire project is built on just a few elements—each track develops across two or three layers at most—and an extremely minimal setup. Often, we are just using everyday objects or small acoustic instruments, which we record and process using a sampler and a laptop. The core idea was to maximize the value of each individual sound and distribute it throughout the space, which inevitably transforms both its signifier and its signified. Both of you have long been interested in sound detached from its original context and meaning. On Structura Parva, the sounds often seem stripped down to traces, gestures and subtle interactions. How do you decide when a sound has been reduced enough, and how do you prevent minimalism from becoming merely an exercise in subtraction? L: For this latest project, each individual sound was developed separately by Angelo and me. We both worked on our own ideas without any prior agreement. After months of work, we decided it was time to meet up and listen to what we had done. Choosing which sounds to use was ultimately quite simple and quick. I don’t know how, but the work each of us had done seemed to share a common goal. A: Honestly, I didn’t really worry about that problem. The goal was simply to find minimal structures that could convey emotional meaning—which, in a way, is a prerequisite for any kind of music. There is almost always a rhythmic element, a background texture or drone, and a melodic element. If you look past the totally hallucinated style, we aren’t actually that far off from a traditional song structure. Angelo’s work frequently explores deterioration, tape processes and feedback, while Luca’s practice involves modular synthesis and improvisation. How has the dialogue between these approaches changed since Forma? Has the balance between improvisation and composition shifted over the years? L: Our approach has always been improvisational. We used to meet for long sessions and then extract the sections that would become the final work. This time, it was different: we worked on the tracks individually, then discussed them and decided together which parts made sense when combined. We then re-recorded them in various environments to give them depth. We also placed great importance on the movement of sounds in space. Therefore, this latest work is much more compositional than our previous ones. A: In this latest work, there is absolutely nothing improvised. We worked in perfect sync on the individual tracks, with each of us utilizing our own sounds and processing techniques. What united us was a shared vision to produce something simple and circular, yet containing an internal evolution driven primarily by how the individual layers intersect. Nothing was left to chance, except for the deliberate use of random modulations and stereophonic automation. The EP is presented as “sounds for night reflections and dark disquiets.” There is a strong sense of restraint and suspended tension throughout the six tracks. Were there particular emotional states, environments or listening situations that informed the album, or do you prefer to leave such associations entirely in the hands of the listener? L: There were certainly external factors that influenced the choice and development of the sound—not necessarily musical ones. In my case, books had a significant impact, changing my approach to life and, consequently, to music. Using a sampler also definitely allowed me to focus more on single sounds. However, I prefer not to give listeners any specific direction regarding our influences, so that their listening experience remains entirely unique and personal. A: The way people interpret tracks is one of the most incredible wonders of music. Because of that, I prefer to let listeners filter the pieces however they choose and place them in whatever context feels right to them. Personally, I feel these sounds express themselves best in a nighttime setting, but that is by no means a strict rule. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by alainPP — Aether, created in 2021 by four friends, initially began as a project for bassist Andrea's final thesis, with the aim of moving away from conventional jazzy sounds. Their sound blends post-rock, contemporary classical rock, and multi-layered jazzy prog."Oort Cloud" is a prime example, fusing ambient, jazzy tones, and dino-tinged progressive rock reminiscent of King Crimson, with a flute buzzing here and there. A long, contemplative suite encourages a dreamlike journey, with a primal Fender Rhodes piano accompanying the oppressive psychedelic guitar riff. "Vogon" opens with Collins' electronic drums, then shifts to a jazzier feel with Claudio Milano's frenetic narration. The air soars on Zappa-esque jazz-rock guitar in the purest tradition, flirting with the great Return To Forever on the distinctive piano; a frenetic finale with infectious energy. "Five Shades, Four Frames" opens with a spacey sound, a prominent rhythmic bassline. A drift into hyperspace follows this encroaching Crimson-esque crescendo; improvisation steers clear of interstellar notes. Midway through, the sound takes on an Arabic quality, reminiscent of a Star Wars desert, over a psychedelic Tangerine Dream melody. The obvious jazzy Rhodes turn on a drumbeat with a hint of Steven Wilson is surprising."The Melancholy of the Little Prince" features a melancholic piano drifting over percussion and electronic notes, giving free rein to the fretless bass. Musical scales, a crackling, distorted sound as if from a parallel universe. "Panta Rei" sees the flute searching for its footing, wandering notes for a learned musical digression; jazz, unmistakably King Crimson, Andrea's guitar surfing avant-garde territory for a controlled jumble. Dynamic and apocalyptic with its explosive contemporary finale, "Swerve" opens with a snowy, religious, ethereal feel. The captivating keyboards lead into post-rock territory illuminated by scores reminiscent of Porcupine Tree. The track then veers into jazzy soft rock territory with a distinctive piano demon unleashing a fury, recounting the new Italian sound.Aether brilliantly dares to create a jazzy post-rock fusion, injecting a dose of ambient and modern prog, opening this movement to the contemporary world.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — After debuting in 2021 with one of Brazil's strangest contributions to the world of zeuhl metal, theJo�o Pessoa based PAPANGU jettisoned the metallic edge of its debut "Holocene" with its follow up"Lampi�o Rei" which followed in 2024 with more of a classic progressive rock approach mixed with thesounds of Brazil ranging from forro, xaxado and udigrudi. The band returns with its Brazilianbravado cocktail of prog and local flavors with its third installment CELESTIAL which features a 10-track concept that once again steers its sound into a new direction. Trimming down from a sextet toa five-member outfit, CELESTIAL follows suit with the metal aspects deemphasized (although stillpresent) and more retro warmth evoked through the use of analog equipment and a passion for bringingthe likes of jazz fusion, symphonic prog, zeuhl and other classic prog influences to this Brazilianstreet party.Another main feature of this third musical expedition is that on CELESTIAL the vocals are ratherdownplayed with crafty instrumental complexities nurturing warm inviting melodies into displays ofprog majesty evoking the elegance of 70s jazz fusion, the artifice of Gentle Giant complexities andthe sneaky labyrinthine excursionist proclivities that nurtured intuited perspicacity throughmusical obstacle courses that never lose their soul and of course all fortified with the true joiede vie that only Brazilian musical styles can deliver. It's a triumphant return to a new form afterwhat sounded to me like a clunky and disjointed sophomore offering. More focused and refined,CELESTIAL may not deliver the supposed concept of a bandit on a mission to prevent an ecologicaldisaster in some undisclosed form but for what the story narrative lacks in heft, the musicalprowess more than compensates for.CELESTIAL may share an album title with the post-metal band Isis but delivers a truer musical vibeof heavenly bliss with the Rhodes piano and vintage keyboard sounds leading the way. Add someunexpected sound effects from a rubber chicken and Brazilian folk instruments and it's easy to getsucked into the majesty of CELESTIAL's intricate flow of modern modern meets retro with a sensiblerunning time of just over 50 minutes. The album's energy bursts into full gear on the opening "Mau-Olhado" and continues its journey of jubilee throughout the album's ten distinct installments. Awaft of classic Canterbury is present throughout evoking the warmth of that classic Egg / SoftMachine / Hatfield & The North along with occasional bursts of heavier rock that emulates blackmetal (at least in the vocal department) all creatively wrapped in the retro prog padding that keepsthe album amazingly well balanced.Tracks like "Fechamento de Corpo" exhibit the band's menagerie of modernity with staccato basedgrooves fortified with crazy contrapuntal effects and a zeuhl-esque propulsion system that allowsthe cadences and motifs to cozy up together snuggly like a den of hibernating mammals. While theprevious works had me wondering if PAPANGU was primarily a one hit wonder with its out of the gatecrashing the prog party debut, CELESTIAL puts those concerns to rest with a beautifully deliveredprocession of tones and timbres executed in crafty compositions that find the band a form ofmaturation that seemed to be lost on "Lampi�o Rei." Throughout this smorgasbord of retro prog onecan detect moments of classic Yes, Genesis, Gentle Giant, Weather Report, Egg and the list goes onhowever PAPANGU also ekes out modernities with excellent production value and 21st century jazzplaybook tricks. While the metal felt out of balance on the previous album, here the subordinateeffects are instigated perfectly without the bombast ruining the dynamic flow. A brilliant thirdalbum here!

items.body: Review by SilverLight59 — Some albums are designed to keep the evening rolling, and others to gently wind the evening down. This one falls squarely in this latter category and does so with style and grace. Bruce Soord requires little introduction. As the anchor behind The Pineapple Thief, he has spent over two decades immersed in the modern Crossover Prog subgenre. His solo work, however, represents a deliberate departure from the intricate full-band dynamics of his main project. This, his third solo release, Luminescence, strips away the technical, rhythmically complex frameworks, propelling percussion and drumming, often associated with the Pineapple Thief to explore a quieter, deeply introspective sonic landscape. While it leans heavily into acoustic textures, incorporates lush string arrangements, and at times runs somewhat in parallel with accessible mainstream structures, the album still maintains a sophisticated harmonic depth that will resonate with fans of atmospheric art rock.If you pay attention to the lyrics, you will find that the album outlines a clear narrative arc, guiding the listener through a journey that begins with the anxious realization of fleeting time on "Dear Life," descends into urban isolation and grief, and ultimately resolves in a peaceful state of closure on "Find Peace". This emotional trajectory is held together by Soord's intimate vocal delivery; his singing style acts as the perfect vessel for his lyrics, conveying an authentic vulnerability that makes the heavy themes feel profoundly personal, and yet he is letting us in. Ultimately, by trading complex rock structures for softer more acoustic arrangements, he has crafted an album defined by its smooth edges and mellow accessibility.So, lets take a brief look at the tracks.Dear Life: The opener here begins with a gentle acoustic strumming pattern, builds a bit to a modest pace, mellow and accessible, and falls directly in crossover territory. Soord's vocals are inviting and emotive. Lyrically, it begins the album's thematic arc of the complexities of life, aging, and the fragile value of one's existence. As a comparison, it might be compared with the melodic sensibilities of Porcupine Tree tracks like "Lazarus." A pretty start. (9/10)Lie Flat: This piece layers atmospheric synth sound beat around Soord's reverbed vocals. It balances a linear vocal melody with unpredictable instrumental textures, isolated guitar work, and periodic forward keyboard sequences. While a restrained work, it will prove to be one of the more dynamic tracks. Again, there is a certain Porcupine Tree & Steven Wilson vocal quality, while the musical structure is bit more in the field of late-era Anathema. Lyrically, it reflects personal clarity and finding unspoken truths later in life. Another very nice track. (9.5/10)Olomouc: Another standout track that begins with sparse acoustic guitar before an expansive, breathtaking chorus section swells into view. The sophisticated orchestration provides the harmonic complexity that provides an engaging depth to the track. The lyrics and chorus are outstanding and memorable. While highly accessible, there is a nice progressive edge delivering this nicely into the symphonic art rock flavor.Another winning track. (9.5/10)So Simple: A very short stripped down piece. Living up to its name, this song relies on a direct, infectious melody. It is arguably the most mainstream friendly track on the record, sacrificing progressive exercises for immediate, pure emotional connection. Compared to the three opening tracks, this seems to be a musical and emotional respite that allows the album twist to some different dynamics to follow. (8/10) Never Ending Light: This track shifts the dynamics with an eerie, slow-burning ambient groove. The keys here have a bit of a sinister edge, the guitars have a bit of discordance and individual tracking creating a fascinating listen. The vocal harmonies and minor-key shifts here evoke a strong Radiohead influence, making it structurally simple but texturally and productionally sophisticated. Another great track. (9/10)Day of all Days: An acoustic-heavy piece that feels like a classic, melancholic Pineapple Thief ballad. Once it build from the acoustic opening, it gains some musical fullness in sections, and then drops back to the acoustic side. This is again an accessible piece that relies on an emotional vocal hook rather than edgy time signature changes. In Addition to the Pineapple thief comparison, one might also see a bit of a parallel to Riverside's softer acoustic moments. (8.5/10)Nestle In: Flirting with a electronica type rhythm, this stands as the album's most upbeat track by a slight margin. The drumming is the most forward here than on any other track in this offering, giving this offering the most propulsion. Not wildly so, but noticeable. There is also a nice guitar amplification near the end, again the strongest of the album. Built on a minimalist, electronic pulse, it bridges the gap between accessible trip-hop rhythms and subtle avant garde art-rock elements. (8/10)Instant Flash of Light: A considerable contrast to the preceding track, this is a haunting sparse song featuring a delicate acoustic center layered with subtle, cinematic strings. It strips away prog pretense for accessible somewhat pastoral sounding singer-songwriter architecture. There is a gradual build in intensity that is refreshing and a highlight, but it still stays well within the boundaries of restraint. This is a nice ballad, but it seems a bit simple compared to the previous tracks. (7.75/10)Rushing: Another track where the acoustic guitar takes center stage, more upbeat this time. Some nice note picking over the top. This picks up the feeling of the song title as there is a push to the flow of the song. As an instrumental piece this seems to serve as a pleasant bridge leading into the concluding portion of the album. (7.5/10)Stranded Here: This Features a slow cinematic build that immediately conjures a kinship with the likes of Sigur Ros both musically and vocally. The slow motion atmospherics provide a satisfying nod to post-rock structures. The gentle acoustic guitar and underlying synth wash and strings are both lovely and immersive. This is easy to get lost in. Another understated highlight (9.25/10)Read to Me: This piece feels born out of the previous as they are similar in tone and tempo. A brief, atmospheric piece that leans heavily into ambient space and sound design. The vocals have an ethereal warmth that is quite alluring, and although very accessible, should appeal even to prog purists who appreciate thoughtful texturing and arrangements. (8.5/10)Find Peace: The closer that brings the record to a wonderful, cinematic conclusion. The slow, soaring strings bring a soft intensity that emphasize the central theme of the album arc, that of letting go and finding inner tranquility. The lyrics and vocals captivate these feelings and leave the listener enlightened and pondering the deeper things of life. The concluding minute winds down with discordant string notes, and the final 10 seconds ends with the opening notes of the first song to create a loop, and so life is, a loop it seems. (8.5/10)Well, what to say? This is a consistently beautiful album in a highly accessible prog and art rock type of way. It could be argued that it is more mainstream than not, but the depth and layering of the tracks suggest otherwise. It is interesting that Soord's solo material is a complete deviation from the bombast of The Pineapple Thief so don't be looking for that here. And there are no epics here. Everything clocks in at three to four minutes or even less. Even so, there is some surprising evolutions within the songs. From a strict progressive rock perspective, Luminescence may come across to some as too narrow in its pacing and overall dynamics. Listeners looking for technical virtuosity, jagged guitar solos, or the complex time signatures of traditional prog may find the record overly safe. The fairly consistent tempo and generally acoustic arrangements if not listened to purposefully may tend to blend together, creating beautiful sonic wallpaper. On the other hand, for those who like a milder form of prog, and are willing to deep dive into it, there is a tremendous lot to like here. One of the album's greatest strengths lies in its immaculate production, pristine sound and mixing, and its emotional honesty. Soord's vocal performance is exceptionally warm, and Andrew Skeet's orchestration elevates the material significantly. Luminescence is a gorgeous testament to Bruce Soord's maturity as a composer, offering a masterwork in atmospheric crossover prog. So, in conclusion, while this may lack the technical fireworks required to satisfy fans of avant-garde or symphonic prog, its pristine sound design, thematic cohesion, and rich textures offer a deeply rewarding listen for fans of modern, atmospheric art rock. In my opinion, highly recommended for those moments when you are looking for some prog serenity. Maybe just slightly under 4 stars, but we will round it up because 3 just simply won't do.

items.body: Becoming a new person Leaving just a trace behind What Nationalists want to avoid That is what I do now Roman Wilhelm began making music in 1991 with the sort of recording setup that encourages either ingenuity or surrender: two ghetto blasters, a teenage bedroom, and no obvious reason to believe anyone beyond its walls would ever hear the results. Born in 1976 in a small West German town, Wilhelm had recorded his first song by the time he was fifteen. A demo tape eventually found its way to a local goth DJ, who invited him to perform at a small dark-music festival. There remained the practical matter of instrumentation. Wilhelm did not own a synthesizer, so he brought his Italian accordion. That solution says quite a bit about the sensibility behind roman946, Wilhelm’s long-running musical project, where the machinery of post-punk and electronic music has always been susceptible to interruption by something tactile, eccentric, or stubbornly homemade. The accordion was hardly an adolescent anomaly. During his years studying graphic design in Halle (Saale), Wilhelm began collaborating with aspiring filmmakers, composing music for images before gradually moving toward a broader conception of performance. After relocating to Berlin in 2005, he found himself drawn into the city’s art world, playing gallery openings and treating music, at times, as an exhibit with its own spatial and conceptual logic. His new album, Balta, gathers those seemingly separate histories into one body of work. Songwriting sits beside electronics; programmed structures are interrupted by acoustic instruments; post-punk economy brushes against folk music and experimental composition. Wilhelm cites Onuka, Laurie Anderson, Lou Reed, The Legendary Pink Dots, and And Also The Trees among his inspirations, a list broad enough to suggest that taxonomy has never been his preferred occupation. The album’s geography is equally expansive. Balta looks toward Germany and Eastern Europe at a moment when political anxiety has become increasingly difficult to leave outside the rehearsal room. Wilhelm addresses the rise of the political right in Germany, intolerance, artistic freedom, gender stereotypes, and the unease surrounding developments farther east, drawing much of the material from events he has witnessed and conversations with people whose lives intersect with these pressures. His working life gives those concerns an unusual proximity. Wilhelm divides his professional time between the German Institute of Economic Research and the Berlin University of the Arts, moving between debates over social policy and questions about artistic independence. Those worlds find their way into songs such as BBC and into the wonderfully peculiar phrase Lead me to Ambivalentopia, which may be as good a name as any for the continent Wilhelm is attempting to describe. Wilhelm speaks eloquently about his songs: The Beach (Daina #1) “The album begins with a Daina, a traditional Latvian genre of song and poetry consisting of four lines, often employing diminutives (Balta, balta debestiņa (little white sky), gaidu, gaidu vasariņu (waiting for the little summer), koki klusē vērojot (trees watching in silence), melnus kuģus jūriņā (black fleet in the little sea)). After the central motif, which uses cellos and guitars to evoke the motion of waves, addresses geopolitical uncertainties, the loud finale resolves the tension through absurd acts of defiance. The final line abruptly switches from English to French and Chinese.” The plodding beat and horns give this spoken word track a deep gravity, almost bordering on psychedelic. Aufbruch “A Jungle rhythm never fully unfolds in this song; repeatedly stutters to a halt, prompting uncoordinated flailing rather than dancing. The bass holds together elements that the piano, synths, and guitar seem unable to reconcile. Hovering over it all is the vocal, which also fails to strictly adhere to the beat. A German story of flight leads to the question of how the grandchild generation would treat refugees today; it identifies intolerant, right-wing behaviour as a negative dimension of flight. Both vocals and lyrics are indirectly influenced by Hildegard Knef and Nico Pfäffgen, particularly in the way they handle the interplay between banality and the dramatic. The song is based on an authentic poem about fleeing Silesia and the subsequent experience of social exclusion in the Federal Republic of Germany.” BBC “This simply structured post-punk theme, driven by a central guitar riff, centers on a person trapped in academic gender clichés.” Chimes and motorik beats bolster this track, which sounds like a lost Fad Gadget track. I Need Nida “A melancholic motif emerges, shaped by the imprecise playing of an analog synthesizer with faulty filters. We observe the protagonist, Katya, a dissident from Kaliningrad as she builds a new life as an artist in her adopted home of Armenia. The abrupt onset of the chorus underscores the fact that homesickness knows no borders. The song was inspired by a text message from the real-life Katya (I asked her where she was going, all she said is: I need Nida).” Ambivalentopia “Berlin-style electro-post-punk meets the stark juxtaposition of multilingual names for various border towns, some situated at the heart of current political events, others far detached from the global stage. The convergence of multiple languages seems to obscure the message, yet invites the listener to seek it out in the spaces in between: the dream of a world where one is no longer limited to simply choosing one out of several names.” This track has a heavily Kraftwerk-inspired chant and backbeat that will get stuck in your head. Exchange; KWC “Being an academic exchange coordinator for Berlin University of the Arts, I deal with the questions raised in “Exchange” on a daily basis: What is openness? How does tolerance emerge? Is time abroad mostly about partying? Where do you go? Is there an atmosphere of openness? Two verses present a caricatured juxtaposition of utopia and dystopia before the language abruptly switches to Chinese in the final chorus. With its hard, driving drum’n’bass sound, “KWC” contrasts sharply with the lyrics: a belated, self-reproachful letter to a deceased friend.” Hotel “An old clock sets the tempo for the album’s most oppressive track; an accordion and an electric piano seem to be chasing the seconds. It tells the true story of a hotelier in a small Saxon town who aggressively tries to justify to the narrator why he did not turn away a group of fascists arriving for a conference (After all, what was he supposed to do? Hardly anyone visited them anymore, and he was left alone with the fascists in the hotel). That clock is ticking very loudly right now, too, in the run-up to the elections in Saxony-Anhalt, where right-wing populist AfD is campaigning for an abolishment of compulsory education, and for the eviction of all foreigners, whoever they may be.” An Old Fort; Take This Town (Daina #2) “Listeners are taken on a spoken-word tour through the overgrown ruins of Kostrzyn (Küstrin). The concluding fragment, “Daina #2,” tells the story of a refugee from Ukraine currently in Latvia (We ordered drinks, I heard her say: “If I don’t drink, I can’t sleep”. Age seventeen). The musical concept, collapses in on itself at the end. Listen to Balta below and order the album here. items.body: Redemption the salvation That’s out of reach All the lies they will forever preach The night belongs to vampires, black leather, bad blood, and decisions best made after the sun has gone down. The Lost Boys sank its fangs into theatres on the 31 of July 1987, and Karlsruhe industrial death wave trio Bleak Monday chose the same date 39 years later to unleash Shelter. It feels like an appropriately cursed bit of calendar alignment. The song and its accompanying video share the film’s appetite for danger, nocturnal excess, temptation, and the enduring truth that everyone looks better once respectable society has locked its doors and drawn the curtains. Bleak Monday takes that invitation underground, descending into a dungeon club where the congregation wears black, the entertainment comes with cages, and somebody has clearly misplaced both the fire code and the holy water. Bleak Monday formed in Karlsruhe in December 2022 with one foot in ’80s wave and the other planted somewhere between metal, industrial rock, and the more bruising end of electronic music. Skinny Puppy, Nine Inch Nails, and Ministry provide useful coordinates, though there is also enough dangerous glamour here to imagine the song turning up midway through a particularly depraved Gregg Araki sequence. Directed by Natascha Gaballo, the video drops Bleak Monday into a dungeon club populated by cages, goth go-go dancers, temptation, domination, and enough black vinyl to make a parish priest reconsider his evening plans. The footage was transferred to VHS and then re-digitized, giving the images the bruised texture of an ’80s B-movie that spent several years behind the counter at a video store before somebody finally asked what was on it. Horror references tied to singer Kim Ryder’s favorite films are tucked into the scenery for anyone inclined to freeze-frame their way through the debauchery. That presentation suits Shelter, a slab of industrial death wave built from Yann Lauer’s guitar, Sebastian “Hubu” Huber’s synths, drums, and bass, and Ryder’s commanding vocal performance. Ryder sings about religious hypocrisy, concealed abuse, televised violence, and salvation sold by institutions that appear to have misplaced the receipt. The central plea for rescue grows increasingly desperate as the song works through shame, faith, exploitation, and spiritual exhaustion. Any promise of redemption feels compromised by the people making it, leaving the singer caught between belief, disgust, and the desire to disappear from a reality that has become unbearable. Gaballo makes that unease physical. Ryder performs amid bodies presented as spectacle, pleasure, threat, and distraction, while the club becomes both sanctuary and trap. The cages are hardly subtle, but subtlety would be rather pointless when the song is throwing death, rape, hypocrisy, and redemption into the room. Sometimes a sledgehammer has admirable editorial instincts. Watch the video for Shelter below: Shelter also serves as a teaser for Bleak Monday’s forthcoming debut album, Bad Music, a title that practically invites hostile witnesses. Since beginning live shows in early 2023, the trio have shared stages with Das Kinn, Nils Keppel, The Body, and Ministry. Judging from this clip, they have already figured out one valuable lesson: if civilization is collapsing, somebody should at least book the dancers. Listen to Shelter below and order the single here. items.body: Statiqbloom Splintered Fingers self-released Fade Kainer’s Statiqbloom has two fairly distinct eras; the electro-industrial years spanning from the project’s foundation in 2014 to around 2020, and the more freeform era (the beginning of which coincided roughly with Kainer’s move to Berlin from Brooklyn) which explore industrialized techno, dark ambient, and rhythmic noise, amongst other sounds. New album Splintered Fingers situates itself between the latter styles handily, unifying them via Statiqbloom’s propensity for blackened textures and depressive ambience. Whether or not Kainer set out to split the difference on the album isn’t clear, but there are plenty of callbacks to his recent history, often reconstituted and recontextualized for effect. “Salt the Flower (stripped back version)” takes the noisy and clamorous cut from recent Hands Production release The Casket Nest and carves away the beats, leaving only reverbed drones, half-chanted vocals and ominous waves of feedback that threatens to drag the whole song under. It’s quite reminiscent of the work he was doing on Winter, although the extremity of its sound, shared by cuts like the brief “Threshold” and the thrumming “Sedated Presence” bring to mind his Kain LP for Sonic Groove. Still, Kainer is ever reluctant to sit still for any period of time, and there are hints of new directions sprinkled throughout the proceedings. Opener “Grave Procession” feels like a classic powernoise cut in its rhythm, but the thick layer of saturation that sits atop its relentless tempo has a sort of smothering tension to it, like the beats are slowly being churned into nothing as the song goes on. Alternately, on “Groundless” the slow tempo and funereal pads have the same sensibility as much of the witch house revival sound, albeit with a nod to the lo-fi sound of early black metal. While not new in terms of sonics, they’re certainly formations we haven’t heard Kainer try his hand at explicitly, and could easily prove to be fertile ground for the prolific artist. Like most of Statiqbloom’s 2020’s output, Splintered Fingers is about mood above all else; even on the record’s centerpiece track “H.O.M.K.V. (live)”, an eight minute excursion into some truly gnarly beats and shouted vocals, there’s a bleak strain of pained emotion that informs the proceedings. Regardless of whatever sounds Fade Kainer is trying his hand at, his particular brand of rage and woe will mark it as his own. 7月になり、歌劇場や音楽ホールが休館すると、オーストリアの音楽界では全国各地のフェスティヴァルが日々の話題の中心になる。まずは4日に、ウィーン3区ホイマルクトで開催された野外イヴェント「オペラの夏」を訪れた（開催期間は7月1～18日）。 服部指揮ウィーン室内管弦楽団による「第1幕への前奏曲」から、踊りや演技でオペラの世界にいざなわれ、その最後の音が鳴ると同時に顔を見せた謎の男は、作曲者のビゼー（ホゼア・ラートシラー）。昨年の《椿姫》でのヴェルディ同様、場面ごとに筋を教えてくれるのだが、本物のビゼーが語っているかのように音楽にまで踏み込んだ解説なので、オペラ通の人が聴いても興味深いものに思われた。 あたりが暗くなってきた前半の最後には、スペインふうの装飾で舞台がライトアップされ、休憩時間の恰好の記念撮影スポットに。後半初め、第3幕への間奏曲ではそのライトアップが暗い岩場を造りだし、ミカエラがカンテラを手にホセを探して回る演出となる（ドミニク・アム・ツェーンホフ=ゼンス）。冷たい夜風が吹きすさび、背景の上方には白く輝く月の画像が…… いままで観てきた歌劇場の舞台以上に幻想的だった。 この日の主な配役は、ナーマ・ゴールドマン（カルメン）、オレステ・コジモ（ドン・ホセ）、ダニエル・グートマン（エスカミーリョ）、ガブリエラ・フルジェニャク（ミカエラ）。時代が変わり、クラシックの存在感が薄れていくウィーンで、多くの人がオペラに出会い、街に美声が流れる機会はじつに貴重だ。2027年には7月1～17日に、ヴェルディ《アイーダ》が上演される。 歴史ある修道院の中庭で観る《サムソンとデリラ》 〈バッカナール〉でデリラを演じるマルガリータ・グリツコヴァ（中央左）© Schark 7月11日には、ウィーン近郊にあるクロスターノイブルク修道院の中庭で上演されたオペラ、サン=サーンス《サムソンとデリラ》を取材した（開催期間は7月7日～8月1日）。このフェスティヴァル「operklosterneuburg」では、昨年から総裁がバリトン歌手のペーター・エーデルマンになり、今年からは独自のオーケストラ「オーパークロスターノイブルク管弦楽団」を擁するなど、多様な変化が起きている。 同じ野外オペラでも、「オペラの夏」との大きな相違は、歌手がマイクを使わない点。壁に四方を囲まれた、840席ほどのこぢんまりした会場なので、生の美声と臨場感を堪能できる。オーケストラが野外のピットにいることは、楽器に対する雨の危険を考えると理想的ではないのだが（雨天の場合は屋内に移るとはいえ、急に降りだして間に合わず、コントラバスを逆さにしたら水がザーッと出たという話を聞いたことがある）、この日は幸い気持ちのよい晴天で、指揮者トーマス・レスナーのもと、素敵な響きを届けてくれた。 マリオ・パヴレ・デル・モナコの演出は、ハンス・クートリッヒの簡素な舞台を最大限に利用して、サムソンが巨大な岩を放り投げたり、神殿の柱を倒したりするスペクタクルを表現していた。今年はフェスティヴァル史上初の大規模なバレエシーンも取り入れられて、きらびやかな衣裳（アンナ=ソフィー・リーンバッハー）とともに、第3幕の〈バッカナール〉を盛り上げた。 デリラ役のマルガリータ・グリツコヴァ、ダゴンの大祭司役セルバン・ヴァシレなど、歌手たちの質も高い。サムソン役のクリスティアン・ベネディクトは、ときおり声が出にくいときがあったようだが、怪力の持ち主に合った容姿と演技によって、観客たちを旧約聖書の不思議な世界にいざなった。2027年7月3日～8月1日の、ヨハン・シュトラウス2世《こうもり》も楽しみだ。

items.body: If a tree falls in the forest, does it make a sound? And what if an entire forest falls? Around Here, The Birds Plant The Trees, inspired by a “clear-felled wasteland” in Leitrim, Ireland, amplifies these questions. In the digital era, it prompts an additional question: “When the liner notes are integral to the release, will listeners intuit the point?” We hope so, in the same manner as those hearing classical works over the centuries have gleaned the intentions of the composers, from “The Goldfinch” to The Four Seasons. In her first work for ensemble, Natalia Beylis uses different instruments to evoke “the rustle of beetles in the hedgerow, the squeak of a leaning Sitka spruce, a lone curlew’s call,” and her overall concern is that listeners will hear the richness of a richness of a landscape and be moved to protect it. While this landscape is incredibly specific: a single field on 12 December 2025, beginning at 6 a.m. ~ it could be any environment threatened by large multinational corporations, who swoop in to offer short-term recompense for long-term loss. Looking out over the field, Beylis notes the activity of a single blackbird, and later, an entire flock. Adding to the pathos is the fact that even birds are now endangered (for details, we recommend Robert Macfarlane & Jackie Morris’ The Book of Birds). If the music of the actual birds is inadequate to promote empathy, might music take up the cause? The alternative is to say nothing and to play nothing. As one might expect, the 51-minute piece is filled with intricate description and high drama. The cello’s low notes launch the piece in a reverent tone, considering at a field that once was a forest. As the other members of the string quartet join in, the nuance starts to develop. What began as drone becomes a harmonic suite with a distinctly Irish lilt. Then the first taps of percussion, like small creatures rustling through the grass, foraging for breakfast. A period of abstraction follows, during which every resident of field and forest receives their own spotlight. The blackbird eats and mates and cross-pollinates. The squirrels rush to and fro; the fox chases the shrew. All the while, the breeze threads through the branches of the hawthorn, creating a rhythm of leaves. The atmosphere seems peaceful until the thrums of the 15th minute, a soupçon of danger as most of the animals and instruments go into hiding. The contrast between presence and absence is integral to the composition. One feels the recession of sound as one might feel the destruction of trees. What was once lush becomes a hush, like the quietude of midday. Then the drone re-develops, a symbol of hope and regrowth. A vast cymbal strike like a gong at 32:07 interrupts the process, leaving only the drums and the wind in its wake. Willie Stewart’s work in this segment is enthralling; it sounds like architecture being built. But as the strings re-enter, are they busy as bees or as bulldozers? The listener is left to decide. Beylis initially planned to “write something to equal the harsh cacophony of the harvesting machines as they shred the nests of fledgling buzzards; to evoke the rumbling shaking noise I’d hear in bed at night as they crashed the huge trees they’d cut to the ground,” but relented for the sake of the blackbird. The dissonance that follows the drums suggests that the idea was not totally discarded. This makes the closing segment all the sweeter: consonance rising out of dissonance, form from chaos. The forest may have been leveled, but around here, the birds plant the trees. This being said, the story is not meant to encourage as much as it is to unsettle. Robert Plant once sang, “if there’s a bustle in your hedgerow, don’t be alarmed now.” Beylis has a different message: be alarmed. Be very alarmed. (Richard Allen)

items.body: There is a certain tenor a WOMAD stalwart comes to expect: a practiced routine, a beaten track past well-known landmarks, a familiarity akin to coming home. Sometimes it’s good to mix it up a bit. This July marked the festival’s first edition in a new location just up the road from Charlton Park, its much-loved site for 17 happy years before taking a break in 2025. Organisers have been quick to reassure returnees that they’ll find the new spot welcoming and Neston Park, just half an hour away in Corsham, does indeed have a home-from-home feel, the flutter of those familiar flags helping crowds settle quickly into the weekend. Some old favourites are missing: the d&b Soundscape stage with its state-of-the-art surround-sound experience; late night party venue Molly’s Bar; the Ecotricity stage, a cosy woodland spot for daytime respite or atmospheric after-dark shows; the magical Hidden Forest lit up by Luke Jerram’s Moon; the World of Science (a niche interest perhaps but a favourite, inevitably, of some). WOMAD kicks off at its brand new site at Neston Park, marking a new chapter for the independent World of Music and Dance Festival – Photo © garryjonesphotography So it is left to the music to carry the show and here the new compactness comes into its own, the smaller tents packed with hidden gems and standout performances of the festival which has not skimped on its musical programme at least. The main stages offer up a mixed bag of hits and misses, occasionally mired by murky sound and drab set design. On the World Stage the effervescent Derya Yıldırım, her voice in turns aching, wistful and full of soul, is supported by the psychedelic squelchy synth and phenomenally groovy rhythm section of her Grup Şimşek. It is sun-drenched and beautiful, augmented by her call for freedom, cultural strength and acceptance for those dwelling in the diaspora. Bristol’s Ishmael Ensemble seem warm in their black outfits, camouflaged against a black stage and backdrop and playing directly into the sun’s heat. Perhaps this explains the low energy feel of both band and scattered crowd. Their jazz-inspired saxophone-and-synth jams with Rituals ‘Orchestra’ (comprising two violins, a harp and a cello) is lacking oomph. A smaller stage may well have inspired bigger vibes. Reggae legend Barrington Levy takes to the World Stage at WOMAD festival – Friday – Photo © garryjonesphotography Reggae icon Barrington Levy is welcomed by a vast, multi-generational crowd and while there are a few unconvincing moments from a seemingly under-rehearsed band (as well as a smattering of problematic lyrical content sometimes associated with reggae that predates the 80s), his voice is as smooth and powerful as ever, his scatting as wild and his strut as convincing, especially on 2025’s ‘A Fi Yuh’. Eventually, the crowd is galvanised into repeatedly requesting “run the track” while Levy teases ‘Black Roses’ and ‘Here I Come’ until well beyond his stage time, berating the MC for clock-watching and singing on until his mic is turned off. The night’s headliner Greentea Peng calls “I love you Barry” and apes his vocal riffing throughout her glorious 90-minute show. An all-round class act, her band provide tasteful support for her elegant, honey-smothered r’n’b, with a high calibre all-female brass section ramping up the energy and spectacle. Greentea Peng headlining WOMAD Festival – Friday – Photo © garryjonesphotography On Saturday, Mixanteña de Santa Cecilia from Mexico City treat a packed Big Top to a classic slice of WOMAD with a high energy fusion of costumed dancers, ritualistic set pieces, eight-piece brass section and percussion. Their mix of cumbia, bossa nova and boleros is full of life, while joyful dancers in long-haired ram-horned headdress and twirling petticoats cause a stir when their bull puppet is sent in to dance with the crowd. It is experiences like these that keep people returning year on year. Similarly, Bénin International Musical provide the perfect sunny soundtrack to a hot afternoon, the disco pop harmonies of Say She She floating across the field give the sense that all is right with this world of music and dance, and Nakibembe Xylophone Troupe are hotly tipped as this year’s mustn’t-miss sensation. Ugandan Nakimbembe Xylophone Troupe bring their 3 metres long embaire to WOMAD, the largest instrument to grace the festivals stages, played by 6 members – Photo © garryjonesphotography But it is the Sunflower stage, a stretch tent conveniently located to break up the just-too-arduous walk between the two main stages, that provides the weekend’s first nugget of pure gold. Tamer Nafar, one third of Palestinian hip hop trio DAM, is flanked for this solo appearance by a beat maker and exquisite Arabic-influenced electric violinist. Nafar is a warm presence with powerful words, throwing out politically charged statements and personal anecdotes with equal emotive power. His latest record, In the Name of the Father, the Imam and John Lennon, references the two CDs his dad would play when driving him to underground rap clubs: the Beatles and the Quran. “But we don’t have to imagine there’s no country”, a defiant teenage Nafar said back then, but he’s retained his love of the seminal Liverpudlians. LYR (Land Yacht Regatta, inexplicably) draw big numbers to that same tent, primarily to catch celebrity poet Simon Armitage in his new musical guise, his downbeat musings backed by pulsing bass and suitably moody, introspective soundscapes. His dry Yorkshire humour goes down well between songs and the crowd responds enthusiastically to the band’s paean to libraries, ‘The Enlightenment’, in particular. Tamer Nafar, a vanguard of Arabic Hip-Hop, the Palestinian rapper living in Israel performs a selection of tracks discussing Middle East politics & life at WOMAD – Friday – Photo © garryjonesphotography The even smaller Village Stage, tucked away in a corner next to second mainstage the Big Top, boasts some of the best acts of the weekend. For only their second live show, Romanian seven-piece Lăutăresele Șaraimanic pull out all the stops with high glamour and captivating dancing drawing on the Turkish and Roma heritage of their homeland. Accordionist Mituș Răducanu, the oldest group member, steals the show with his delighted toothy grins. Later in the day, Belarusian Yegor Zabelov keeps the audience riveted with his expansive world-building, pushing the accordion to new creative limits with drones, sound walls and percussion sounds. And sparky Portuguese solo artist Ana Lua Caiano grabs attention with her melodramatic delivery, then holds it with impressive looping of synth, percussion and voice into multilayered epics of fiery emotion. A stunned audience of all ages watch each song construction with awe, then explode in applause as Caiano expresses her deep delight and gratitude. Lautaresele Saraimanic at Village Stage performing at WOMAD Festival – Friday – Photo © garryjonesphotography The sentiment was one that emanated across the site as another WOMAD was put to bed. Dynamic, welcoming, vibrating with fighting spirit and above all full of joy and connection, the 2026 edition served as a reminder of the role the festival plays in building community and educating through creativity. Pre-sale tickets for 2027 have already sold out. Perhaps this year’s success will instil organisers with the confidence to bring back some of the site’s sorely missed old favourites; or, more in keeping with the culture of the event, to surprise us with something wholly new and unexpected.   Pre-sale tickets for 2027 have already sold out, but you can keep in the loop for the next batch over at womad.co.uk     Photos © garryjonesphotography The post Event Review: WOMAD 2026 @ Neston Park (Corsham, Wiltshire; Thursday 23rd to Sunday 26th July 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: “Natural” moves at walking pace, a lovers rock groove kept soft under Clarence Bekker‘s blues-trained voice as it eases across the rocksteady sway. The new single from his Barcelona band is a plain love song from a singer with a long, loud history behind him. Bekker carries an unusual CV for a reggae singer: a UK chart entry in the 1990s as CB Milton, seven world tours, and a spell fronting the street-recorded Playing For Change project. Born in Suriname and raised in the Netherlands from the age of six, he cut his teeth in the Dutch group Swinging Soul Machine before that dance-pop run, then settled in Barcelona and, in 2016, built a band around local players. That band is a five-piece of Barcelona regulars: guitarist Francisco Guisado, known as Rubio, keyboardist Arecio Smith, bassist Charlie Cuevas and drummer Carlos López behind Bekker’s vocals. They hold a weekly Thursday residency at the jazz club Jamboree and have carried the same lineup as far as Australia and Brazil. The song came together between Barcelona and the road, Bekker recording while Irish lyricist Michael Leahy sent words over from wherever he was travelling, a habit going back to their fax-machine days writing CB Milton hits together in the 90s. Everyone in the band had a hand in it, and it holds to the idea in its title: an unhurried love song, played the easy way. It is the first single from an album due later this year. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — If there is one characteristic Jean-Luc Ponty has always possessed, beyond his skills as a performer and composer, it is his instinct for surrounding himself with great musicians. Following his experimental period with the "Experience" and the Open Strings album (a highly successful venture), he embarked on what would become the first in a series of eight albums with a band, one that, despite some lineup changes, created an enduring body of work that was progressive in the broadest sense of the word, helping to expand the genre's boundaries and lay the foundations for its future.Upon the Wings of Music could also be interpreted as leaning on his musical mentors, Frank Zappa and John McLaughlin, after crossing the Atlantic; he had collaborated with both, and they were the ones who definitively (and fortunately) brought him into the realm of jazz-rock fusion. He was accompanied by Patrice Rushen on piano, keyboards, and synthesizers; Ralphe Armstrong on bass; Leon "Ndugu" Chancler on drums (who had played with Santana); and guitarists Dab Sawyer and Ray Parker Jr.Upon The Wings Of Music already showcases his compositional style, featuring solos built upon progressions with well-defined starting and ending points, as well as space for his musicians to shine, all of them collaborating to develop not just one, but several musical ideas. This approach incorporates the hallmarks of classic jazz-rock alongside funk (a genre in which Rushen specialized, playing the clavinet)."Question With No Answer" showcases an acoustic side, featuring piano and a cleaner sound, evoking the image of wood silhouetted against the snow. There are touches of rustic violin, accompanied by the band with a more organic jazz feel that works just as well, leaving room for controlled improvisation.Jean-Luc would distort the violin like no one else, making it feel like a guitar, while retaining the lightness and volatility inherent to the instrument itself, resulting in a completely unique sound. This accounts for the originality of his albums and his sonic style, with compositions crafted specifically for his instrument and playing technique. "Polyfolk Dance" is one of the most ambitious tracks, employing polyphony before launching into a violent, fast-paced section where the soaring high notes allow the Rhodes to make themselves felt, and the wild guitar cuts like a knife while Ralph Armstrong's ever-present bass closely backs it up. (Live, this track lasted eight minutes, three minutes longer than the studio original.)Another distinctive feature is how the violin can also sound like those soaring, sustained Minimoog solos, reminiscent of Chick Corea, allowing him to function as an entire band on his own, backed only by the rhythm section. Waving Memories also holds various melodies within, some distinctly rock-oriented and even psychedelic, others taking on a spacey feel through classic progressions. The interplay between Ponty and Rushen is unmissable, and the violin reaches notes that make us see the constellations.One can discern not only the logical influences of the Mahavishnu Orchestra but also those of the early Passport, with the violin stretching out much like Klaus Doldinger's saxophone, as evidenced in "Fight For Life." This marked a mature debut for the band, setting the stage for a repertoire destined to evolve and expand further during this second phase of his career, his most personal era, and one that afforded him the time and space to truly stretch out, both literally and metaphorically.

Languirand's followed the trend of other synth wizards by playing all ofthe intruments himself and bothers to sing (+/- acceptably so) , but what comes out of the ordinaryis Pascal's use of the Moog Taurus, giving an amazingly deep bass tone. Languirand had majored in cinematography from Concordia University and a lot of his tracks were accompanied with small films.Opening on the cosmic Alpha 700, we already know we're about travel into the upper layers of thesky, and the Taurus bass pedals are used in a very singular manner, ricocheted by his searingguiter. You'll find the same kind of climate in Oiseau de Crystal and Megalopolis. Orient has acelestial mood gruising over India's troposphere, which is so�ewhat of a departure, but it won't bethe only one.On the flipside, we have a weird atypical folky tun that doesn't fit with the rest of the album, the7-mins Dans Le Vent, where Pascal gives voice orally. The closing 12-mins Omega is a minor tour deforce, making you think of Crazy Diamond's unearthing, but shaped by Schulze or Froese. Somewhere stuck between Heldon and Schulze with a pinch of Floyd, Minos has its own distinctiveflavour and is well worth the detour to look for it (none of his album have been reissued in CD,however).

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — Fruupp, for years lived under the shadows of giants, as an opening act for bands like Genesis orKing Crimson, working hard to get recognition, the quintet was prolific in every sense of the word,and despite never getting any commercial success, some of their influence can be felt on genres suchas math rock or symphonic prog.Before the actual review starts, I'd like to take a moment to do something I am not acostumed to inthis site, I'd like to give the band some extra points for their wonderful sleeve art, which is aninteresting mix of medieval, impressionist and dadaist styles...unlike many eclectic covers whichare absurd for the sake of absurdity itself, this cover is absurd but also hides intention andartistic quality, anyone dedicated enough to aesthetics will get what I mean. It's a beautifulsleeve indeed.Starting off with that which is the absolute strength of this record : It's creativity and uniqueapproach. Northern Ireland had been a colony under British imperial rule for quite a while at thatpoint, so it's natural that aspects of cultural syncretism are to be felt across the 39 minutes ofmusic this album has, yet, it keeps most of the Irish musical identity intact, this is an act ofcultural resistance, but mixed with a proper dose of syncretism, it feels innovative, if they hadgone a little more British, then it would have hit the uncanny valley, yet this is not the case. Iwas quite surprised to learn that this band is not Iberian either, since strangely enough some ofthe modes, scales and rhythmic patterns are borrowed from Iberian music, this adds to a refreshingMediterranean sound mixed with strong Celtic influence, it's quite funny how well these two stylesfit together in the record, since it *shouldn't* be that way as their almost opposite philosophiesin the way they approach this art. I also noticed some faint Arabic influences, but they are smalland barely noticeable, it's on tracks such as "Graveyard Epistle" where it can truly be felt...butit might as well just be the Iberian influence I mentioned before, since iberia is stronglyinfluenced by the Arab world due go the 700 years it spent under Arabic rule.The quality of the compositions is rich and diverse, despite being relatively short (between the 4and 8 minutes mark), they have several small movements, leitmotifs and variations, it's rhythmicallydense and that's it's clearest identity factor, across the record, the intricate and delicatepercussions, bass lines and guitars are condensed in a dance and struggle against each other,pushing to their limits and then coming together in complex polyrhythms, metrics and lines thatsyncopate and then go into chaos, over and over, it's hypnotic! The track "Song for a thought" is agreat example of this, it also incorporates classic Rock and roll elements. Then comes theambient textures, oboes, string ensembles, delayed and reversed guitars and some clicking cymbals createan ambience of immersion and psychedelia which is ethereal in nature, it induces a high state ofconcentration and doesn't contradict the complex rhythms, if anything it complements them.If I had to describe the sound of this record in a single sentence it'd be : Baroque andmulticultural, vanguardist yet hypnotic...feels fresh even in 2026, which is 50+ years since it'srelease.The musicianship is great, and there's a natural chemistry between them all that holds thecompositions together like a glue, they are technically prominent (although not gifted) and have agreat sense of melody and rhythm, their teamwork is astonishing, specially the lead singers voicewhich is similar to Lake from ELP and Shulman from gentle giant. The production is okay, it doesfeel rough and noisy at times but putting this into context (underground act mainly known by collegestudents in Britain) it's understandable, it's something you can overlook if you will, andprobably will do so anyways because of how hypnotic this all is.Fans of gentle giant will love this since it feels a lot like "Acquiring the taste" (specially theslower, violin driven parts), the similarities are astounding, the band had not yet reached theirfull identity yet, but it's enjoyable anyways.A solid 5/5!

items.body: A pair of heavy hitting body music tours set to make their way across North America this fall ended up booking shows in Vancouver on the same day, and thankfully have been folded into one supercard, meaning that in a couple of months we’ll be getting to see Spike Hellis, Normal Bias, Buzz Kull, and Kontravoid all on the same night. A complete murderer’s row of modern EBM to be sure, but if you’re in NA you’ll likely have a chance to check out one if not both component parts as they’re extensive tours covering most of the continent. Hell, Spike Hellis is already on the road in support of the killer LP which finally dropped last week. Check the dates and grab tickets while listening to this week’s tracks. Are you Knormalled enough? Soft Vein, “Another Summer” Did you listen to our interview with Soft Vein on the podcast last week? If not, you should go do that right now, then come back here and listen to the exceptional “Another Summer”, yet another absolute stunner from the forthcoming All We’ve Known of Heaven. Justin Chamberlain’s songwriting, intimate style of performance and instrumentation keeps getting more undeniable with each release, and given the massive leaps he’s made in a mere three years, the overcast but beautiful skies are the limit for this melancholic LA based artist. One of our most hotly anticipated albums this year. All We've Known of Heaven by Soft Vein Patriarchy, “Bite Marks” Patriarchy are the enfants terrible of modern American darkwave, an act that provokes on stage and on record with each release. The thing is, the material backs it up, with last year’s excellent Manual For Dying showing off just how good the LA trio fronted by Actually Huizenga has gotten at bringing their gnarly stage show to their records. New EP Appendices is no different, featuring five tracks of mechanized shock rock and electro, expect to hear “Bite Marks” on your stompier dancefloors soonish. Appendices by Patriarchy Caustic, “Not Going Anywhere (Klack mix)” North American cult industrial impresario Matt Fanale follows up his last double LP Fiend with a remix album Unfiended, featuring a diverse roster of collaborators including Male Tears, Petrol Bastard, Alien Faktor, and Mark Pistel (!!!) amongst others. Of course Matt’s other project Klack dips in, bringing some of that new beat NRG to “Not Going Anywhere”, resolutely funky and full of more orch hits than a synclavier sample library. Giddy up! UNFIENDED by Caustic ner.ogris, “A View” German acts ner.ogris (or ner\ogris) have won us over via one LP and one EP of rock-solid electro-industrial which opts for considered grooves and sculpted sound design rather than shock or excess. This brooding taster from forthcoming LP Femme Fatale gets their strengths over quickly and artfully and bodes well for another course of proper home cooking from the pair. FAME FATALE by ner.ogris Knormalled, “The Servitor” The second EP from Indianapolis producer Knormalled shows a canny knack for a moody hybrid of dark electro and EBM which puts a premium on mood and slowly sliding timbral colour. Thru might best be appreciated as a full EP listen, but you can get a decent sense of the vibes from this shuddering slice. Should likely appeal if you’ve dug recent records by Kurs, or are still burning a candle for Distorted Memory. KNORMALLED THRU by Knormalled Ikon, “The Witness Tree” Some nice and easy summer goth rock from the always understated Aussie masters Ikon. Somewhat confusingly previewed then withdrawn, “The Witness Tree” is the first new material from Chris McCarter & co. in a few years and is setting up a forthcoming singles collection covering the entirety of the McCarter helmed era of the band. B-side’s got some dreamy pep, too. The Witness Tree single by IKON The post Tracks: August 10th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Band: Nostalghia | Album: Departure | Genre: Progressive metal | Year: 2026 From: Mexico City, Mexico | Label: Independent For fans of: Opeth, Enslaved, Riverside Bandcamp Nostalghia is a one-man project helmed by Mexican multi-instrumentalist Alex Becerra. This album is my first exposure to Nostalghia, but it looks like this is a very prolific project. According to RYM, this Departure is Nostalghia’s 14th release since their debut in 2020. The music on this record is stunningly diverse and ambitious. Aside from the band’s black metal roots, jazz, classical, alt-rock, classic prog, and more all play important parts here. “Leaving” opens the album on a restrained note. Acoustic guitar lines weave around one another in a way that draws from Baroque composers. When the vocals enter, they’re restrained. Rattling percussion, anxious strings, and tinkling piano build a sense of claustrophobia before suddenly cutting out and giving way to a melodic, piano-led passage that flows directly into the more-immediately-impactful opening of “Dearly Departed”. Riverside and Enslaved are both obvious influences in this song, with rapid, wiry guitar runs and vocals that vacillate between soulful and harsh. Latin jazz emerges about midway through as a nice bit of contrast. Many acts attempting such an incorporation come off as hokey and ham-fisted, but Nostalghia’s composition feels coherent and thought-out. The opening of “Uróboros” features some chamber music influence alongside restrained proggy folk, akin to acts like Jordsjø or Änglagård. When metal eventually emerges, there’s a wonderful, blistering solo supported by rich string arrangements. This sort of metal-classical hybrid is a not-uncommon trope in the realm of prog, but few acts pull it off this well. “Qa Muqu”, sung in a Mayan language and directly adapted from the Popol Vuh, has a peppy, jazzy opening. Enslaved-flavored black metal propels this piece along, with brass and piano exclamation points throughout. During instrumental passages, jazz once more comes to the forefront, and time signatures and rhythms get wonky as hell. The transitions between heavy and gentle moments are often sudden, but it all feels earned. Somber piano opens “Wherever You Are”. This is a mellow piece overall that gives the listener some appreciated breathing room. Riverside, Porcupine Tree, and Dream Theater’s better slow songs are all clear influences on this piece. “The Abyss Whispered” jumps back into metal, and tinkling chimes give it a celestial, otherworldly feel. The arrangements of the different parts of this song are diverse and complex, with some parts leaning into harsh black metal and others utilizing dissonant modern classical music. The final song on the album is the 10-minute “Offret (including “Ashes upon Eden”, “By the Corpse of Earth” and “Mercy”)”. “Ashes upon Earth” is led by clean guitar and pulls in elements of classical and dark folk music. I especially get flashes of some of Agalloch’s mellower output here. As distortion builds, so does the sense of majesty, before suddenly cutting out in the transition to “By the Corpse of the Earth”. Muted, atonal strings pluck and plink awkwardly and hauntingly, like the score to a horror film. Rattling chains and distant piano add to the ambiance. In the hands of less-skilled composers, this movement could easily become grating, but Becerra sells the tension and the anxiety. The final movement, “Mercy”, leans heavily upon ethereal atmospherics, with angelic vocals lifting everything skyward. Departure is a moving piece of music that displays an impressive breadth and depth of musical knowledge and skill. The songs demonstrate complex and technical instrumental ability, while the structures manage to be both diverse and coherent. The fusion of jazz and classical feels impressively natural, and I know there is a ton to discover upon repeated listens. Score: 92/100

items.body: Three Sunsets Over MarsfieldLP, Album, Limited EditionFaraway Press – FARAWAY PRESS 18UK2010Three Sunsets Over MarsfieldLP, Album, Limited Edition, SlipcaseFaraway Press – FARAWAY PRESS 18UK2013 Flavour text written by Brendan Walls for the press release:"Shortly after the Second World War, a medical facility for returned soldiers was built in the small town of Marsfield.The patients were in some way incapacitated by that great and monstrous war; some missing limbs, some deafened or blinded by explosions, others driven out of their senses.A few muttered old military secrets, a few sang long-forgotten ballads, a few built small ships inside milk bottles; others walked the corridors and grounds, scanning every dark corner for an unseen but ever present enemy.It was not an unhappy place; there was a sense of deep friendship amongst the patients, bound as they were by the collective hell of battle. One of the most popular amongst the men was Lieutenant Wilson. He was no more than a Lance Corporal but earned the nickname Lieutenant during his stay at the home. Wilson had the remarkable ability to receive radio signals through the metal plate in his head. He would touch a metal window frame or steel bed head, incline his head at oblique angles, open his mouth and a sort of popping static would emanate from within his dark mouth. Subtle manipulations of his jaw, the inclination of his head or his physical location in the room would alter the signals he received.As it happened he was the longest surviving member of the facility. When it was decommissioned in 2000, he was to be moved to a neighbouring hospital to see out his final days. Wilson resolutely refused to be moved. Barricading himself in his room, he declined food, water and medical attention until he was eventually moved to the west wing of the home and cared for by a rotation of staff members from the nearby hospital. He finally passed away in the later months of 2002 when this album was recorded."Recording info supplied in newsletter from Faraway Press.

大阪市の京橋駅近くにあるオープンイノベーション施設「QUINTBRIDGE（クイントブリッジ）」。NTT西日本の本社ビルの敷地内に2022年に創設され、世の中をもっとよくしたいと考える人々が集い共創する場として、ワークショップやモノづくり、入居する会員の事業が行われている。 この「新たな出会いフロア」と呼ばれる1階で、5月15日、「部活動（吹奏楽）の地域展開を考える ― 地域と企業がともに描く、これからの“文化の支え方” 」と題するイベントが開催された。 部活動の地域展開とは 文科省が主導する部活動改革の一環。教員不足の原因のひとつとされる教員の長時間労働を是正するための「教員の働き方改革」に端を発し、「部活動のガイドライン」で活動時間などの制限について目安が提示されたうえ、公立中学校の部活動を教員に負担させないために、運営主体を地域（民間）に「展開」しようと各自治体が中心となって進められている。 すでに「改革推進期間」の3年間を終えて、2026年度から6年間の「改革実行期間」に入った。現状、休日については、過疎地域を中心に多くの地域で実施されはじめているが、平日に関してはさらに課題山積で、ごく一部の地域での実施に留まっている。 減少が危惧されている吹奏楽部の課題 吹奏楽部は、もっとも地域展開が難しい部活動とされている。 なぜなら、楽器や楽譜といった「備品」や、音出しが可能な「練習場所」は、学校部活動の練習環境だからこそ毎日のように使用できるものだからだ。学校の音楽室は、体育館のように独立した建物でない場合がほとんどなので、地域クラブの運営者が利用する場合は、セキュリティの問題を解決しなければならない。 また、吹奏楽にはおもに12種類の楽器があって、本来それらの指導ができる「専門人材」も必要だが、これまでは教員の献身的な努力を中心に、先輩が後輩を教える伝統的なスタイル、場合によっては外部講師を招くということで、何とか成り立たせてきた。 そのほか、コンクールや演奏会での「楽器運搬」費などもあり、活動費は運動部よりも高額になりがちだ。これまでは自治体からの補助金などで工面できていた部分があるが、地域展開して国や自治体の予算が不足している現状のままであれば、習い事の月謝と変わらない金額を受益者（保護者）が負担することになるだろう。そうすると、子どもが入部できるかどうかは親の判断にも左右されて、吹奏楽ができる子どもが限られてしまう。 こうした課題が横たわる吹奏楽部の地域展開だが、だからと言って、このままでよいという話にはならないだろう。急激な少子化により、1つの学校では合奏できる人数に満たない地域も増えているうえ、教員不足を解消するには働き改革が急務だからだ。 小中学校の団体数や部員数の減少を数字で説明 未来のクラブ活動の姿を民間の事業が提案！ さて、こうした課題に対して、QUINTBRIDGEのイベントでは民間企業、行政、学校の立場から、さまざまな解決案が提示された。筆者は後日に記録動画を拝見したのだが、どの登壇者もプレゼンテーションの熱量が高くて面白く、ポジティブに未来を捉えた発表だったことは、まず言っておきたい。 民間からは4人が登壇し、画期的なテクノロジーやサービスが紹介された。 まずは「離れていてもtonari（隣り）で過ごそう」というキャッチコピーで他のシステムと一線を画す遠隔コミュニケーションシステム「tonari」。床から天井までを映す大型スクリーン、タイムラグを感じることない通信技術、そしてカメラを意識せずに目線を合わせて等身大の相手と話ができるスクリーン内蔵型カメラを備える。吹奏楽の現場であれば、リモートでの指導や合奏が自然に行えるのではないかと期待が膨らんだ。導入コストの高さが課題だが、普及するのであれば、生徒の移動や楽器運搬の問題が解決でき、地域格差の是正につながるだろう。 NTT西日本グループからは、全国20以上の自治体と連携して社会実装を進めている自動運転EVバスが紹介された。山口県周南市では、2024年度から実証実験がはじまり、すでにNavya Mobility製の自動運転EVバスが街を走っていて、満車のことも多いという。バスやタクシーのドライバーの高齢化や不足を改善するだけでなく、生徒の移動手段として利用できる日も近いかもしれない。 そのほか、服部管楽器が学校にある「休眠楽器」を修理して格安にレンタルすることを検討していること、また、就活支援と企業の人事コンサルティングを行うHUB@LIFEが、「仕事ができる人に吹奏楽経験者が多い」と企業にアピールし、スポンサーになってもらいつつ学生とつなぐ場としてコンサートを開催していることを紹介した。 この日の登壇者を紹介するスライド 地域クラブを大人のバンドの下部組織に 学校や地域の現場からは、すでに動き出している事例として、まず西宮市立中学校の教員・吹奏楽部顧問が、外部に受け皿となる組織をつくった例が紹介された。 大人の吹奏楽団の下部組織に中学生対象のジュニアバンドをいくつかの地域につくり、当初から指導者を用意して演奏会など本番の予定も組み、活動をパッケージにして提示。これにより、生徒や保護者の活動への不安が軽減できたとのこと。 「どこかのジュニアバンドが縮小しても、バンドを統合したり、小学5年生から社会人まで入れる大人のバンドが受け皿になって、子どもたちの活動は守られる」と語った。前述したような吹奏楽ならではの課題はあるものの、指導者など大人たちのつながりによって支えられる好例となるかもしれない。 学校を「まち」に ！ 地域住民にも活動の場をつくる北海道安平町 自治体からは、北海道安平町教育委員会の教育長である井内聖氏がオンラインで登壇。安平町は人口は7000人ほど、小学校1校、中学校1校のほか、小中一貫の義務教育学校が1校あるが、子どもも大人も減り、スポーツ・文化に取り組む機会も減っている。この機会を支援するため、学校内に「まち」をつくった経緯や現状を語った。 安平町立中学校の部活動は令和7年度までですべて廃止にして、地域クラブの練習場所、時間、送迎、活動費については教育委員会が主導して調整を図った。地域おこし協力隊と総合型スポーツクラブが、スポーツ・文化活動の運営をサポートし、希望する指導者や教職員の兼職兼業によって指導者を確保。中学生だけでは成り立たないので、小学生から大人まで多世代のために環境構築を進めた。 このプロセスで、令和5年4月に義務教育学校として新設される予定だった安平町立早来学園をどのようにつくり、地域に開放するかが議論された。 この学校の空間デザインを担当したのが、デジタルアートのクリエイティブで知られるチームラボだ。顔認証によるセキュリティを導入するなど、テクノロジーを活用して、大中2つの体育館や図書館、家庭科室のほか、音楽室、美術室、技術室といった学校施設を、公民館のように地域とシェアし、ほぼ毎日9時から21時まで地域の人が簡単に利用できるようにした。 顔認証システムを導入し、地域住民が自由に出入りできる安平町立早来学園の図書館の様子が映し出された たとえば、平日の日中に学校内で、シニアの健康教室、子育て支援、料理教室などが開かれ、0歳から90歳が集うなか、休み時間には学校の子どもたちも本を借りに来る。昼休みに図書館で弦楽四重奏のコンサートを開き、シニアやお母さんと赤ちゃんといった地域住民に加え、先生、生徒が自由に集まり、食いつくように演奏を聴く――そんな自然に交流が生まれる光景も映像で紹介され、孤立や分断のない「まち」の姿の一つだと感銘を受けた。 吹奏楽部は今年度から地域クラブになり、この学校内で活動している。中心となる外部講師だけでなく、各楽器の講師も協力して指導にあたり、オンラインレッスンも活用している。今年は小学生1名を含む15名が所属。遠くから通う子どももいるため、平日16〜17時は自主練習、17〜19時で合奏などの全体練習を行い、保護者の理解も得ながら順調に活動しているそうだ。 ここに至るまでには、現場との意見の相違もあったそうだが、井内氏は「10年後のスポーツ・文化環境は、どうなっているだろうか」と関係者に問いかけ、「残すために」必要な形を模索していった。井内氏は、予測できない未来をどう予測するのか、「無理・難しい」の先にあるものは何か、それが吹奏楽がなくなるという未来であれば、私たちはそれを受け入れるのか――そう訴え、理解を得ようと努めたそうだ。 現状を変えることはエネルギーがいるが、まわりの変化が激しいなかで、何も行動しないことは逆にリスクになり得る。多くの地域住民が学校になごやかに集い、中学生だけでない多世代で多様なクラブ活動が行われている安平町の映像からは、この判断によって町全体の幸福度も高まったのではと感じられた。 オンラインで登壇した、北海道安平町教育委員会の井内聖教育長 財源を確保しながら、民間の力で魅力ある地域展開を 昭和の時代から続いてきた日本の部活動文化は、学校教育の一環としてその意義を評価されてきた。文科省の「部活動改革及び地域クラブ活動の推進等に関する総合的なガイドライン」（2025年12月）にもあるように、地域クラブになったとしても、その教育的意義は守っていくことが望まれている。 ただ、日本のスポーツ・文化や教育への投資が諸外国と比べても少なく、地域展開についても予算が不足している状況のなか、この改革の負担を現場の運営者や指導者、保護者に強いれば、スポーツ・文化は衰退してしまう（すでに小中学生の吹奏楽団体・人口は、明らかに減少している）。 公教育の一環として子どもの「機会均等」を守るためには、今回QUINTBRIDGEで発表されたような民間のアイデアを活用できるように、まず行政がしっかりと財源を確保しなくてはならないだろう。それが地域全体も活性化するような「魅力ある地域展開」に導くことになるのではと考えさせられる機会だった。 おカネがかかる芸術教育〜国際比較から考える日本の課題と活路

2026年の最大のニュースは、メインプログラムがこれまでの2日間から3日間へと拡大されることだ。初日9月11日の夜は、毎年フェスティヴァルの締めくくりを飾ってきた音楽祭メインコンサートが、祭典の幕開けへと据え直される。 東京都交響楽団を指揮するのは梅田俊明。仙台フィルハーモニー管弦楽団の常任指揮者を6年にわたって務め、国内の主要オーケストラへの客演を通じて、堅実かつしなやかな音楽づくりを聴かせてきた。メインコンサートの初登壇となる今回、その円熟した手腕がどのような響きを引きだすか、楽しみだ。新国立劇場合唱団の緻密で広がりある合唱と、金森穣率いるNoism Company Niigataの圧倒的で洗練された身体表現、そして都響とが立体的に織りなす公演となるだろう。 続く12日と13日には、0歳から入場できる「OK！オーケストラ」が両日開催へと拡張され、親子で楽しめるダンス公演「動物たちのダンス＆ミュージック」も新企画として登場。 さらに昨年好評を博した子どものためのオペラ『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』も再演され、家族で味わえる本格的な舞台体験が広がる。SaLaDワークショップやアンサンブルレッスン、ヤマハと共同開発した「だれでもピアノ®」など、聴くだけにとどまらない参加型コンテンツの厚みも、この音楽祭ならではの特徴だ。 多摩・島しょ地域へと届けられる「OK！ オーケストラ in 多摩」や「SaLaDプレミアムコンサート」も今年さらに充実し、街と街、人と人、世代と世代をやわらかにつなぐ。秋の東京に、音楽の喜びが響き合う3日間がやってくる！ 音楽祭メインコンサート《Boléro》～ 音楽と舞踏の豪奢プログラム 好評の《ボレロ》は今年も目玉の一つ。華やかに名曲たちが奏でられる ©サラダ音楽祭実行委員会 「音楽祭メインコンサート《Boléro》」は祭典の幕開けを飾るにふさわしい、豪奢にして緻密なプログラム。指揮を執るのは梅田俊明である。NHK交響楽団や読売日本交響楽団など国内主要オーケストラと共演を重ねるヴェテランの登壇は、本音楽祭にとっても新たな色合いをもたらすに違いない。 昨年SaLaDプレミアムコンサートを指揮した梅田俊明が今年はメインを振る ©K.Miura 前半はグリーグ「組曲《ホルベアの時代より》」で北欧的な清冽さを響かせ、続くラター《グローリア》では、新国立劇場合唱団の輝かしい歌声が天井高くこだまするだろう。後半はラヴェル「組曲《マ・メール・ロワ》」が鮮やかなオーケストレーションで物語を紡ぎ、Noism Company Niigataとのコラボレーションが始まる。 そして、いよいよラヴェル《ボレロ》へ。サラダ音楽祭の象徴的演目ともなりつつあるこの演目は、Noism Company Niigataの舞踏が、凛々しく力強い身体表現で東京都交響楽団とのコラボレーションを展開する。希望や光を感じさせる音楽と舞踏の圧倒的世界に、聴衆は再び息を呑むことになるだろう。 OK！ オーケストラ～0歳から入場OK！ 家族みんなで楽しむ1時間 0歳から入場可能な「OK！ オーケストラ」では、指揮者体験コーナーも実施予定 ©サラダ音楽祭実行委員会 0歳から入場可能なオーケストラ・コンサート「OK！ オーケストラ」は、毎年大好評を博してきた人気プログラムだ。今年は土・日の2日間開催へと拡大される。タクトを振るうのは川瀬賢太郎。その伸びやかな音楽作りで、子どもから大人まで魅了する指揮者だ。司会には子ども向けTV番組でおなじみの小林顕作、ダンスは近藤良平率いるコンドルズ、児童合唱は東京少年少女合唱隊と、舞台はにぎやかな顔ぶれで埋め尽くされる。 指揮を担当する川瀬賢太郎は1児の父。「幼少期に本物の音に触れる体験の大切さ」をたびたび語っている ©Tomoko Hidaki プログラムもじつに贅沢だ。すぎやまこういち「交響組曲《ドラゴンクエストV》」から、ビゼー《カルメン》、ロッシーニ「《セビリャの理髪師》序曲」、シャブリエ《スペイン》まで、子どもも大人も心拍数が上がるような名曲がずらり。指揮体験コーナーや、客席も一体になって歌うコーナーもあり。声を出しても、身体を動かしてもOK！ 家族みんなで音楽の喜びそのものを体感する、かけがえのない1時間となるだろう。 子どものためのオペラ『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』（日本語上演）～ 色鮮やかな冒険ファンタジー 『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』は自然と楽しめる曲が散りばめられており、子どもにも親しみやすいオペラとなっている ©サラダ音楽祭実行委員会 意地悪なトロールの女王に連れ去られたしろくまのヴァレモンを追って、心優しく勇敢な少女ラグナが冒険の旅へと踏み出す──昨年大好評を博した東京芸術劇場制作の子どものためのオペラ『しろくまの王さま ヴァレモンの物語』が再演される。 ヴァイオリン、クラリネット、トロンボーン、ハープ、打楽器という小さなオーケストラが、北欧の森や吹雪の山々を色鮮やかに描き出す。楽しく笑える場面も多いが、歌手たちの確かな歌、彩り豊かな照明、そして衣裳は、まぎれもなくオペラそのもの。子どもが新しい世界と出会い、大人が童心に帰る一時間である。 サラダ音楽祭2026 公式サイト

多様性のあるレパートリーの構築を目指して、日本と英国を拠点に活動。東京藝術大学音楽学部附属音楽高等学校を経て同大学音楽学部器楽科卒業、同声会賞を受賞。英国王立音楽院修... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る 夏のロンドンはシーズン・オフで、演奏会はBBCプロムスに集中する。本稿ではプロムス全体のプログラムを見渡しつつ、閑散期の隠れた名演をレポートしたい。 今年のプロムスではアメリカ合衆国建国250年を記念して、アメリカ系の作品が例年より多く登場する。しかしガーシュウィンやコープランド、バーンスタインら一部の作曲家に偏っていることは否定できまい。なお山田和樹は、バーミンガム市交響楽団とジョン・アダムズの合唱作品《ハルモニウム》に臨む。 プロムスらしく随所に散りばめられた現代作品のなかには、ベッツィ・ジョラス（『音楽の友』2026年8月号でレポート）やジェシー・モンゴメリー、ジョーン・タワーなどアメリカ系作曲家の作品も見受けられる。しかし作曲家のジェンダー比率の均衡を図った結果、存命の作曲家では女性表象のアーティストが多い。権力勾配の不均衡を是正するクオータ制のやりかたでいえば、マイノリティ属性の人数をいったん増やすのは正解だが、西洋クラシック音楽の場合には「死んでいる作曲家」の扱いも工夫できるはずだ。平たくいえば、もっと「歴史上の女性」と「いまを生きる男性」を入れないと不都合をこうむる世代ができてしまう。 本来プロムスが始まって間もない20世紀前半は、エセル・スマイスの歌劇《The Wreckers》やドロシー・ハウエルの交響詩《Lamia》が人気を博すなど、女性作曲家は「そこに普通にいた」。歴史を踏まえて見ると2026年のラインナップは生ぬるい。 むしろ今年頻出するのはR・シュトラウスで、《ツァラトゥストラはかく語りき》、《死と変容》、《アルプス交響曲》や「歌劇《ナクソス島のアリアドネ》」に「《ばらの騎士》組曲」、そして《英雄の生涯》、《4つの最後の歌》と充実。またベルリオーズが「序曲《ローマの謝肉祭》」、《幻想交響曲》、「レクイエム」、《ファウストの劫罰》と並ぶのは珍しい。 プロムスといえば、大編成の金管や打楽器を浴びるように聴くのが醍醐味で、先の2巨頭に加え、エルガーやヴォーン・ウィリアムズ、ウォルトンの交響曲、そして初日に奏でられたフィンジ《聖チェチーリアのために》といった英国の大規模作品は、この音楽祭ならではの聴き応えがあろう。 また今年はマーラーも交響曲が5曲とたっぷり聴けるが、ブルックナー作品がゼロで寂しい。なおプロムスはBBCのサイトでラジオ中継を配信しており、日本からも無料で再生可能だ。 BBCプロムスのメイン会場、ロイヤル・アルバート・ホール ©原田真帆 ロンドンを拠点とする楽団の首席奏者たちが室内楽を奏でる「チェンバー・プリンシパルズ・オブ・ロンドン」 そんなプロムス開幕前夜。ウォータールー駅の高架のふもとにある 1901 Arts Club にて、チェンバー・プリンシパルズ・オブ・ロンドンの演奏会を聴いた。この団体はロンドンを拠点とする楽団の首席奏者によって構成されており、メンバーたちがふだん奏でる大規模な管弦楽曲とは打って変わって、より親密な室内楽の公演を実施している。 この夜はロイヤル・オペラ・ハウス管弦楽団のコンサートマスターであるセルゲイ・レヴィティンと第2ヴァイオリン首席のヤン・シュモルクが、2台ヴァイオリンのために書かれた楽曲で鮮やかに魅せた。 まずは定番のルクレール「ソナタ」から「第4番」で開始。日ごろバレエ・ダンサーを支えているだけあって、舞踏家ルクレールの音を絶妙に引き出していく。かと思えば、シュポア「デュオ・コンチェルタンテ第2番」では、まるで管弦楽を聴いているような錯覚に陥る。 そしてシュニトケ《Moz-Art》ではコントさながらの演技力を見せる。演奏の前に奏者が台詞を言っていたのだが、楽器を鳴らしてもそれが言葉の続きのようで、ふだんから共に演奏しているからこその音のせめぎ合いは演劇のごとし。 終曲のハルヴォルセン《ノルウェー民謡による演奏会奇想曲》は、ふたりが代わるがわる協奏曲の独奏と伴奏を務めているかのようだ。通常は歌劇場のピットのなかで繰り広げられる職人技に、45人弱の小規模会場で間近に触れる贅沢な時間だった（7月16日）。
